units.translation: “When the first parts of the sun come together with Leo, then the loud Etesian winds fall thickly upon the broad sea.” Apollonius also adds the reason why they blow in summer. For when the deified Dog Star was scorching the Cycladic islands and there was a long period of drought and crop failure, the inhabitants of Ceos, in accordance with an oracle, summoned Aristaeus, the son of Apollo and Cyrene, from Phthia. He took some men from Arcadia and came to Ceos, and established a sanctuary of Zeus Icmaius for the sake of bringing about rains, and he propitiated the Dog Star, and he ordained that the Ceans should annually watch for the rising of the Dog Star in arms and sacrifice to it. Hence the Etesian winds blow, cooling the earth in summer, and the Greeks were relieved from drought. About Cyrene, Pindar relates in the Pythian Odes (IX) that she remained a virgin for a long time and hunted with Apollo. Once, while wrestling with a lion, she was loved by Apollo; he seized her and carried her to the place now called Cyrene in Libya after her, and having intercourse with her he fathered Aristaeus. Pherecydes (3 fr. 58 J.) and Ariaethus (fr. 4 M. IV 319) say that she was carried on swans, by Apollo's design, to Cyrene, while Agroetas in the first book of his Libyan History (fr. 2 M. IV 294) says she was brought by Apollo to Crete, and from there to Libya. Cyrene's sister was Larisa, after whom a city in Thessaly is named. Some say that Cyrene was the daughter of Peneus, wrongly; for she tended flocks by him, but she was not his daughter. Mnaseas (fr. 39 M. III 156) says that she went to Libya of her own accord, not conveyed by Apollo. Acesander in his work On Cyrene (fr. 5 M. IV 285) relates that when Eurypylus was king of Libya, Cyrene was brought over by Apollo; and when a lion was ravaging the land, Eurypylus offered the kingship as a prize to whoever killed the lion, and she killed it; and her children were Autuchus and Aristaeus. Phylarchus (81 fr. 16 J.) says that she came to Libya with a larger group; and when they were sent out to hunt, she went out with them. Some trace the lineage of various Aristaei, as also Bacchylides (fr. 62 B. III 587 = 45 Blass-Snell): one was the son of Carystus, another of Chiron, another of Earth and Heaven, and the one from Cyrene.

b. That the Etesian winds blew at the request of Aristaeus, who was the son of Cyrene, daughter of Hypseus, and Apollo, and brother of Autuchus. But he in Libya 〈...〉, while Aristaeus in Ceos first discovered beekeeping and the processing of olive oil. And having invoked the Etesian winds, Zeus Aristaeus was called also Apollo Agreus and Nomius.
